title: Nimbus Financial - Redwood Console tracing / request logs debugging walkthrough
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs focused on debugging production failures for Nimbus payment flows. AE intro, SE demo of traces, request log export, search/filters, error grouping, and suggested guardrails. Discussed SSO, audit logs, data residency, and potential pilot scope (dedicated vs hosted). Agreed next steps: provide security pack, sample request logs export, and trial onboarding checklist.
action_items: Owen Chen - share sample request log export (anonymized) and a short script to reproduce a failed payment flow - due 2028-07-19
Lena Park - send security packet (SOC2, ISO docs, KMS integration notes) and pricing for a 3-month pilot - due 2028-07-15
Jonas Becker - provide example failing request IDs/trace ids from last week - due 2028-07-14
next_steps: Redwood to send security/compliance packet and pilot pricing
Nimbus to attach sample request IDs and confirm pilot scope (hosted vs dedicated)
Schedule follow-up technical deep dive (SE-led) next week to run live request log export and reproduce error)
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2028-07-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Owen Chen (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sara Lopez (Nimbus EM), Jonas Becker (Nimbus Platform Eng), Priya Shah (Nimbus SecOps), Alan Wu (Nimbus SRE)

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm lena from redwood, appreciate you making time. quick intro, i'll hand off to owen and marco to walk through the console tracing and request logs stuff — we've seen this help customers debug intermittent failures in payments flows.
[00:12] Sara: thanks lena, hey all, sara here. main goal is to understand how we'd find the failed payment requests and the root cause quickly, and what level of access we need. we have compliance questions too.
[00:24] Owen: awesome. quick agenda: tracing UI, error analysis grouping, the request logs export, and then a short live debugging flow using a sample trace. i'll try to reproduce last week's failure pattern but we'll use an anonymized example.
[00:34] Jonas: quick note, we run on a mix of hosted endpoints and some dedicated pools for night-batch jobs. our latency budget is pretty tight — 200ms p50 for authorizations.
[00:44] Owen: got it. that'll affect batching and cache choices, we can point to which traces show latency spikes from batching windows.
[00:51] Marco: also, just to flag, we often see KV cache misses that look like they cause repeated re-computation. sometimes the transcript tools misread KV cache as "KV cash" so apologies if the auto transcripts are off.
[01:03] Priya: and from security, we want to confirm audit logs and KMS integration for customer-managed keys if we go private.
[01:12] Lena: yes we'll cover that in the Q&A. ok owen you're up.

--- Tracing UI Walkthrough ---
[01:25] Owen: opening the console — top-level trace list. you can filter by model, route, or request status. here's a trace where we had a 502-like response from the model model-v2-quant, you can see the timeline across steps: routing, kv-load, compile, token-generation.
[01:40] Owen: (click) the waterfall shows a big stall during the "kv fetch" step, about 180ms. that's where we see the cumulative latency. you can expand node details to see hardware and kernel choice.
[01:56] Sara: is that hardware attribution reliable? sometimes our infra tags are off.
[02:01] Owen: it's based on the routing event and the host metadata — occasionally labeling is fuzzy if the host hasn't reported labels, so you'll see host-unknown. we advise instrumenting the host metadata push.
[02:13] Jonas: can we link trace ids back to our internal request ids? we annotate client side.
[02:18] Owen: yes — we have a request_id mapping field and you can search traces by client_request_id. also there's a copy-to-clipboard link for trace_id.

[02:30] Owen: next, error analysis. console will surface grouped errors by signature and stack-ish info for the runtime step. here's an example of an "unexpected EOF" during streaming — group count 23 in the last 24h. you can click into the group to see representative traces.
[02:47] Marco: the grouping uses a fingerprint that is somewhat heuristic — so sometimes groups split across similar chevrons, i mean similar exceptions.
[02:57] Sara: do you capture model-level debug strings or is that PII?
[03:03] Owen: by default we capture structured error codes and a short model message; we redact request content by default for hosted, but in private/dedicated you can configure retention and whether to capture full payloads (subject to compliance).

--- Request Logs and Export ---
[03:20] Owen: here's the request logs view. you can filter by timeframe, route, status, client_id, and search free text. exports support CSV and ndjson with trace_id, request_id, status, latency_ms, route, model, and error_code.
[03:36] Jonas: can we include our own headers/metadata? we currently send X-Org-Id and an internal correlation id.
[03:41] Owen: yes we index common headers. if you add the header to the SDK call it becomes searchable; for older requests you can still match on client_request_id if it was present.
[03:50] Alan: how long are logs retained?
[03:53] Owen: hosted default is 30 days, configurable for Dedicated and Private — enterprise plans can go longer or push to your S3/Kafka via streaming.
[04:03] Priya: for security, do audit logs record who accessed a specific trace?
[04:08] Owen: yes audit logs capture console access, API key usage, and user-level actions; in Private you can integrate with your SIEM and our audit events include trace_id references.

[04:20] Owen: live repro — i pulled an anonymized failing trace. i'm going to open the trace, show the request payload (redacted), and step through the retry loop.
[04:31] (screen share noise)
[04:36] Owen: you'll see three attempts; attempt 2 shows a 500 from the runtime step with an error_code "model_timeout", attempt 3 succeeded after fallback to a smaller quantized model.
[04:49] Sara: ah so fallback happened automatically?
[04:51] Owen: yep if you configure fallback policies we can route to a cheaper / faster compatible variant when latency or capacity thresholds are hit. you can set rules by route.
[05:00] Jonas: does fallback preserve session state / kv cache?
[05:04] Marco: when switching model variants the KV cache isn't always compatible; we surface cache-mismatch warnings and you can choose to warm the new variant first. sometimes that leads to slight content drift.
[05:17] Sara: that explains the weird validation failures we saw.

--- Debugging Flow ---
[05:25] Owen: now i'll show how we'd go from an alert to root cause: alert triggers on error-rate spike, click from alert into the grouped error, open a sample trace, jump to request logs, export the set, then run the repro script locally.
[05:38] Jonas: for the repro script, what infra do we need? can we use your SDK or do we need a special token?
[05:43] Owen: standard API key with read-only access to logs is fine for export; for replay you can use the SDK with a test key, we provide a sanitized payload script.
[05:52] Owen: (typing) showing the export job — it runs async and posts a download link to the console and to an email we configure.
[06:02] Priya: is the exported data encrypted at rest?
[06:05] Owen: yes, encrypted using our storage keys; if you use Private with customer-managed KMS we can use your CMK.
[06:13] Sara: we need to run a small pilot. what would you recommend: hosted trial with increased retention or spinning up a dedicated pool?
[06:22] Lena: for an initial pilot, hosted with a dedicated route and increased retention for the debug window is the fastest. if you need strict data residency or CMK, Private is the next step. we can propose both in pricing.

--- Security / Compliance Q&A ---
[06:34] Priya: does redwood do SOC2?
[06:36] Lena: yes SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001, and we have pen test reports. i'll include the packet. we also support SSO (SAML/OIDC) and RBAC in the console.
[06:47] Priya: and can we restrict who can download exported logs?
[06:50] Marco: yes, audit policies and RBAC rules control export permission; every export is an audit event with actor, time, and trace_id references.
[06:58] Priya: perfect.

--- Performance and Costs ---
[07:05] Jonas: curious about cost impact of long retention and tracing depth — will that spike our bill?
[07:10] Lena: retention and debug depth are charged separately; request logs export bandwidth and storage are billed. Redwood Optimize can recommend sampling rates and caching strategies to reduce cost — we can run a cost projection for your request mix.
[07:22] Sara: can Optimize recommend quantization profiles for our payment model?
[07:26] Owen: yes, based on latency and quality targets we suggest quantization and batching settings; we'll share an initial config after we see the sample logs.

--- Wrap up / Next steps ---
[07:35] Lena: recap: we'll send security docs and pilot pricing, owen will share an anonymized request log export and repro script, and nimbus will share failing request ids. schedule follow-up SE-led repro session next week.
[07:48] Sara: sounds good. one small ask — could you include a short runbook for on-call to triage these traces?
[07:55] Marco: yep we'll add a 2-page runbook with common patterns (kv cache miss, model_timeout, fallback behavior).
[08:03] Lena: thanks all, we'll follow up via email with links.

(There are typical transcript artifacts: occasional mis-hearings, filler words, and partial overlapping speech; timestamps are approximate and inserted every 15-60s in the UI export.)

End of recording.
